title: AI That Uses Your Computer: What Screen-Control Agents Can and Cannot Do
summary: Computer-use agents can now click, type, and navigate your screen. Here is what they actually automate today, where they fail, and what to check before giving one your credentials.
before: You describe a task in words, and the AI gives you instructions to follow yourself. The AI never touches your screen.
after: You describe a task, and the agent sees your screen, moves the mouse, types, and completes the workflow autonomously.
body:
Something shifted in early 2026: AI agents stopped just answering questions and started doing things on your computer. These systems can see your screen, move your mouse, click buttons, fill forms, and complete multi-step tasks while you watch. The promise is simple: describe what you want done, and the agent does it. The reality is more complicated.

## How Computer-Use Agents Work

A **computer-use agent** operates through a perception-action loop. It takes a screenshot, sends it to a vision model that interprets what is on screen, then executes an action like clicking or typing, and repeats. Unlike traditional automation tools that follow rigid scripts, these agents can adapt when layouts change or unexpected pop-ups appear.

The major players work differently under the hood. Claude's browser extension and computer use API rely on screenshot analysis combined with reasoning. OpenAI's approach, now integrated into ChatGPT Agent after the standalone Operator product was shut down in August 2025, uses a similar vision-and-action cycle. Google's Project Mariner prioritizes DOM awareness over raw pixel parsing, making it stronger on web workflows. Open-source options like Browser Use, with over 94,000 GitHub stars, let you run similar capabilities with your choice of underlying model.

## What They Can Actually Do Today

These agents genuinely work for certain tasks. Repetitive browser work like filling forms, collecting data from dashboards, and organizing files are their sweet spot. One documented case showed an agent extracting data from 847 rows in 3 minutes versus 2+ hours of manual copy-paste. They can navigate websites, compare prices, schedule appointments, and handle multi-step research workflows.

Claude's browser automation includes a confirmation step for major actions like bulk deletion or unsubscribing. ChatGPT Agent lets you schedule recurring tasks and access them across devices. For developers, these tools can verify front-end implementations by clicking through an app the way a real user would.

## Where They Fail

The limitations are consistent across products. CAPTCHAs stop them cold. Two-factor authentication requires you to step in. Complex JavaScript interfaces, drag-and-drop functionality, and intricate calendar systems still confuse agents regularly. Payment transactions and banking are off-limits by design.

Speed is another issue. Browser automation is inherently slow because it must wait for pages to load, JavaScript to execute, and the DOM to render. An agent completing a task that takes you 30 seconds might need several minutes of screenshot-analyze-click cycles.

Benchmark scores tell the story. The best computer-use agents score around 82% on OSWorld, a standard benchmark for desktop tasks. That sounds impressive until you realize one in five attempts fails. On complex workflows, reliability drops further.

## The Security Question

This is where things get serious. A computer-use agent can click buttons, delete files, send emails, and execute commands using your credentials. Every session you are logged into, the agent can access.

**Prompt injection** is the primary concern. An attacker hides instructions on a webpage, invisible to you but readable by the agent. Your agent visits the page, follows those hidden instructions as if you typed them, and acts using your active sessions. In August 2025, researchers found that hidden text on a webpage caused an agent to extract a user's email and one-time passcode. No malware required, just text on a page.

The platforms building these tools have added safeguards. Claude requires confirmation for high-impact actions and asks permission before accessing new apps. ChatGPT Agent uses "watch mode" requiring supervision on sensitive sites and refuses banking transactions entirely. But these measures reduce risk rather than eliminate it.

## What to Check Before Trusting an Agent With Your Accounts

Before you let any computer-use agent access your logged-in sessions, ask these questions:

- **Does it sandbox actions?** Running agents in isolated environments like virtual machines or containers limits the blast radius if something goes wrong.
- **What confirmation steps exist?** Look for products that pause before irreversible actions and let you review what the agent plans to do.
- **Can you audit what happened?** Some agents provide screenshots and logs of every action. Others do not. If you cannot review what the agent did, you cannot catch problems.
- **What sites should be off-limits?** Keep agents away from banking, email, and anything with stored payment methods until you have high confidence in the system.

Run any new agent manually at least three times before scheduling it to work autonomously. Introduce small variations and see if it recovers gracefully.

## Where This Is Heading

Computer-use agents are the least capable versions you will ever use, and that is both exciting and a reason for caution. The technology is improving quickly, but for now, treat these tools as powerful assistants that require supervision rather than autonomous workers you can fully trust with sensitive accounts.

For more context on how these agents fit into the broader landscape of AI systems that take action, see our explainer on agentic-ai-explained. The underlying models powering these agents continue to improve, as we covered in state-of-llms-q2-2026.
